request.system: You are a senior clinical coder in an Australian public hospital with fifteen years of experience coding inpatient episodes in ICD-10-AM. You are careful, conservative, and you never invent a code you are not sure of the chapter for.

messages.content:
Code the episode of care below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed. Give the three-character ICD-10-AM category for the principal diagnosis.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Age: 53
Gender: Male

Hospitalization Dates: [redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient initially presented with acute myocardial infarction and underwent percutaneous coronary intervention with stent implantation. However, residual stenoses and stent malappositions were observed, and the patient was referred for CABG. Echocardiogram revealed a left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 19%, and enhanced computed tomography showed bilateral occlusions of the internal thoracic arteries and a small fragile sternum after sternoturnover fixation. Left thoracotomy was performed without cardiopulmonary bypass, and the saphenous vein and radial artery grafts were successfully anastomosed to the target vessels. The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged on postoperative day 12.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 53-year-old man presented with acute myocardial infarction and underwent percutaneous coronary intervention with stent implantation. Residual stenoses and stent malappositions were observed, and the decision was made to perform CABG due to the left anterior descending artery, high lateral branch, and left circumflex artery lesions. The patient had a left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 19%, a bilateral internal thoracic artery occlusion, and a small fragile sternum after sternoturnover fixation, which made the left thoracotomy approach the preferred method. The procedure was performed successfully without cardiopulmonary bypass, and the patient had an uneventful recovery, resulting in a patent bypass graft of all target vessels. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 12 without any issues.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The admission being coded is the CABG episode. The AMI and PCI were earlier, and the patient was referred for CABG because of residual stenoses and stent malappositions. The conditions responsible for this admission are the coronary lesions in the LAD, high lateral branch and left circumflex, so this is coronary atherosclerotic disease.

An acute MI (I21) is coded to an episode of care within 4 weeks (28 days) of onset. If the CABG was part of the same or a continuing episode within that window, I21 could apply. The summary says "presented with acute myocardial infarction and underwent PCI", then "referred for CABG", which suggests a transfer or a later admission. The stated reason for CABG is residual stenoses of the coronary vessels, with no ongoing AMI treatment described. The conservative choice is therefore chronic coronary artery disease, I25 (chronic ischaemic heart disease, including atherosclerotic heart disease of the native coronary arteries).

The alternative is I21 if this is still within 4 weeks and the AMI is considered the current condition. In ICD-10-AM, I21 applies to an AMI of 4 weeks or less, including when the patient is transferred, and is still coded as I21 on the subsequent admission. This is a close call. The details point to an elective-style CABG with a 12-day postoperative stay, a complicated planning process (ITA occlusion, sternum fixation) and a detailed workup, which suggests it was probably not the same admission as the AMI. I will go with I25.

CODE: I25
